## Why the best teams win

The model trained on 256 knockout team-seasons to predict progression, achieving a mean within-season Spearman correlation of 0.45 with a 95% interval from 0.34 to 0.54. It placed 46.7% of actual finalists in its top 4 ranking, compared to the 23.9% a random ranking would achieve; the 95% interval for this share ranges from 30.0% to 60.0%, which lies entirely above the random baseline. The model's Brier score was 0.098 against a base-rate guess of 0.103, yielding a skill score of 0.05 with an interval from -0.04 to 0.13 that includes zero, rendering the edge inconclusive. Pedigree, results, and style feature sets overlap in their predictive power rather than differing significantly. Style emerges as the most important driver, led by Attacks per game with an importance of 0.229, followed by Goal difference per game at 0.198. Long passes (% of passes) is a conditional stat that helps only alongside other variables, while Fouls committed per game (lower is better) is model-dependent and unstable.

## Winners vs runners-up

Comparing group/league-phase stats between winners and runners-up across 15 finals reveals no significant differences in the first four statistics examined. Pre-season UEFA club coefficient showed a mean difference of 0.57 with a Holm-adjusted p-value of 0.111, while Fouls committed per game (lower is better) had a mean difference of -1.13 and a p-value of 0.181. Shots per game recorded a mean difference of 0.79 with a p-value of 0.292, and Pass accuracy (%) showed a mean difference of 0.76 with a p-value of 0.422. Since all these Holm-adjusted p-values exceed the significance threshold of 0.05, none of these differences are statistically significant. The data indicates that while style metrics like Attacks per game drive deep runs in the model, the specific group/league-phase profiles of winners and runners-up do not differ significantly on these early indicators.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Teams beaten (%)' figures say how many teams the club did better than on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where doing better means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Use 'significant' or 'significantly' only for a Holm-adjusted p-value comparison, never for other differences. Write plain markdown without tables.

Write 350-450 words of markdown in total, two paragraphs of about 90 words under each of exactly these two headings, in this order:
## Why the best teams win
## Winners vs runners-up

Explain which stats are associated with deep knockout runs and whether pedigree, results or style matters most, using the feature-set comparison in a sentence or two without quoting its intervals: they overlap, so present the differences between pedigree, results and style as tentative (say 'overlap', not 'overlap significantly'). Say how well the model does by comparing its Brier score with the base-rate Brier score and stating what share of the finalists were in its top 4 against the share a random ranking would give; give each model-quality number that has a 95% interval together with that interval. For the Brier skill and the top-4 share the facts say whether the interval includes its no-skill value: where it does, say the model's edge on that measure is inconclusive; where it does not, say which side of that value the whole interval lies on. Never call the model's edge significant or superior. 'Importance' is the average size of a stat's push on the expected stage, in either direction. The model learns from the knockout team-seasons, using each team's group/league-phase stats: give the knockout count, not the group/league-phase count, as what it learns from. Report findings only: end each section on a finding, with no summary or implication, and do not explain how SHAP or the model works. Only call a stat 'robust' if its robustness label is robust. A 'conditional' stat helps only alongside the other stats (on its own it points the other way or barely at all) and a 'model-dependent' stat is unstable: describe each that way. Winners vs runners-up compares those same group/league-phase stats, not what happened in the final; discuss only the first four stats in that comparison and no other stat from it (it is sorted from smallest to largest Holm-adjusted p) and say whether any difference was significant. Never call a winners-vs-runners-up difference significant unless its Holm-adjusted p is below the significance threshold in the facts.
